answers: Commonly known for protecting the President, the Secret Service also plays a leading role in investigating and preventing financial and electronic crimes. To accomplish its mission, the Secret Service relies heavily on the use of IT infrastructure and systems. In 2009, the component initiated the IITT investment—a portfolio of programs and projects that are intended to, among other things, improve systems availability and security in support of the component's business operations. GAO was asked to review the Secret Service's oversight of its IT portfolio and workforce. This report discusses the extent to which the (1) CIO implemented selected IT oversight responsibilities, (2) Secret Service implemented leading IT workforce planning and management practices, and (3) Secret Service and DHS implemented selected performance monitoring practices for IITT. GAO assessed agency documentation against 14 selected component CIO responsibilities established in DHS policy; 15 selected leading workforce planning and management practices within 5 topic areas; and two selected leading industry project monitoring practices that, among other things, were, in GAO's professional judgment, of most significance to managing IITT. The U.S. Secret Service (Secret Service) Chief Information Officer (CIO) fully implemented 11 of 14 selected information technology (IT) oversight responsibilities, and partially implemented the remaining 3. The CIO partially implemented the responsibilities to establish a process that ensures the Secret Service reviews IT contracts; ensure that the component's IT policies align with the Department of Homeland Security's (DHS) policies; and set incremental targets to monitor program progress. Additional efforts to fully implement these 3 responsibilities will further position the CIO to effectively manage the IT portfolio. Of the 15 selected practices within the 5 workforce planning and management areas, the Secret Service fully implemented 3 practices, partly implemented 8, and did not implement 4 (see table). Within the strategic planning area, the component partly implemented the practice to, among other things, develop IT competency needs. While the Secret Service had defined general core competencies for its workforce, the Office of the CIO (OCIO) did not identify all of the technical competencies needed to support its functions. As a result, the office was limited in its ability to address any IT competency gaps that may exist. Also, while work remains to improve morale across the component, the Secret Service substantially implemented the employee morale practices for its IT staff. Secret Service officials said the gaps in implementing the workforce practices were due to, among other things, their focus on reorganizing the IT workforce within OCIO. Until the Secret Service fully implements these practices for its IT workforce, it may be limited in its ability to ensure the timely and effective acquisition and maintenance of the component's IT infrastructure and services. Of the two selected IT project monitoring practices, DHS and the Secret Service fully implemented the first practice to monitor the performance of the Information Integration and Technology Transformation (IITT) investment. In addition, for the second practice—to monitor projects on incremental development metrics—the Secret Service fully implemented the practice on one of IITT's projects and partially implemented it on another. In particular, OCIO did not fully measure post-deployment user satisfaction with the system on one project. OCIO plans to conduct a user satisfaction survey of the system by September 2018, which should inform the office on whether the system is meeting users' needs. GAO is making 13 recommendations, including that the Secret Service establish a process that ensures the CIO reviews all IT contracts, as appropriate; and identify the skills needed for its IT workforce. DHS concurred with all recommendations and provided estimated dates for implementing each of them.

**Summary of the Secret Service IT Management Report**

The U.S. Secret Service (Secret Service) plays a critical role in protecting national leaders and safeguarding the nation’s financial systems. To support these missions, the Secret Service relies on a robust IT infrastructure and a skilled workforce. This report evaluates the Secret Service’s management of its IT portfolio, workforce planning, and the performance of its major IT investment, the Information Integration and Technology Transformation (IITT).

**IT Oversight and Acquisition**
The Secret Service has made significant strides in centralizing IT management. Following the hiring of a full-time Chief Information Officer (CIO) in 2015 and the consolidation of IT staff under this role in 2017, the CIO has fully implemented 11 of 14 selected IT oversight responsibilities. These include developing a strategic IT plan and participating in departmental governance boards. However, the CIO has partially implemented three key responsibilities. Specifically, the Secret Service has not fully established a documented IT acquisition review process, which led to the failure to review two IT contracts totaling approximately $1.75 million. Additionally, the Secret Service’s enterprise governance policy does not fully specify the CIO’s role in budget formulation, and the CIO has not mandated that agile projects measure product quality or post-deployment user satisfaction.

**Workforce Planning and Management**
The Secret Service faces challenges in effectively managing its IT workforce. While the component has substantially improved employee morale through initiatives like student loan repayment programs, it has minimally implemented leading practices in strategic workforce planning. The Secret Service has not fully identified all required technical competencies for its IT staff, nor has it regularly analyzed the workforce to identify skill gaps. Consequently, the Secret Service has not fully implemented targeted recruiting strategies or a comprehensive training program. The report notes that the Secret Service has not established metrics to track the effectiveness of its recruitment efforts or to assess the impact of its training programs.

**Performance Monitoring of IITT**
The Secret Service and the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) have effectively monitored the performance of the IITT investment. The Secret Service conducted regular reviews of the IITT’s Enabling Capabilities program and Multi-Level Security project, identifying and addressing schedule delays. For the two agile projects—Uniformed Division Resource Management System and Events Management—the Secret Service successfully tracked velocity and development progression. However, the Secret Service has not yet fully measured post-deployment user satisfaction for the Uniformed Division Resource Management System, though it plans to conduct a survey by September 2018.

**Recommendations**

This report evaluates the Secret Service’s implementation of IT oversight responsibilities, workforce planning practices, and performance monitoring for the IITT investment.

**IT Oversight and Acquisition Management**
The Secret Service has made progress in centralizing IT management, consolidating all IT staff and assets under a Chief Information Officer (CIO) appointed in 2015. However, the CIO has partially implemented three key responsibilities. Specifically, the Secret Service has not established a documented IT acquisition review process, which led to the failure to review two IT contracts (valued at approximately $1.75 million) in a recent sample. Additionally, the Secret Service’s enterprise governance policy does not fully specify the CIO’s role in budget formulation, and the CIO has not ensured that agile projects measure product quality or post-deployment user satisfaction.

The Secret Service faces challenges in managing its IT workforce. While the component has substantially implemented practices to improve employee morale, it has minimally implemented practices in strategic planning, recruitment, and training. The Secret Service has not identified all required technical competencies for its IT workforce, nor has it established a reliable process to assess staffing needs. Consequently, the Secret Service lacks a comprehensive analysis of workforce gaps and has not implemented metrics to track the effectiveness of its recruitment efforts. However, the Secret Service has not fully measured post-deployment user satisfaction for the Uniformed Division Resource Management System, a gap the agency plans to address by September 2018
